newsitem.title: USA: Motorola Q1 seen lower than year ago, up from Q4.
newsitem.headline: Motorola Q1 seen lower than year ago, up from Q4.

text.p: Motorola Inc's 1997 first-quarter earnings are expected to be lower than in the same period a year ago but higher than fourth-quarter profits, as the company battles to recover from a downturn in its key semiconductor business, analysts said.
Analysts said the quarter-to-quarter sequential growth in earnings was a sign that the company's other businesses, such as cellular phone infrastructure, were holding up.
"Generally, semiconductor industry sales are down...and that's going to be the big driver in lower earnings year-over- year," said Robert Wilkes, analyst at Brown Brothers Harriman.

According to First Call, the consensus of analysts' estimates for the first quarter is $0.45 a share, down from $0.63 earned in the 1996 first quarter, though higher than the $0.39 reported for the fourth quarter and the $0.34 for the third.

Analysts said Motorola's cellular infrastructure business appeared strong, and they see further growth ahead. Motorola invested heavily in code division multiple access (CDMA) technology, a digital wireless phone system that provides greater call clarity and network capacity than analog systems.
The company has systems in Asia and recently announced a major contract in Japan.

"CDMA is turning out to be a very good investment," said Chris Chaney, an analyst for A.G. Edwards, adding the company had been criticized for betting on CDMA because it was slow to attract customers.

Its cellular handset division, hit with stiff competition and declining prices, likely benefited from sales of the small StarTac phone, a technology used internationally and domestically, analysts said.
To be sure, some analysts are doubtful that the company will meet first-quarter earnings expectations.

Eric Buck, an analyst for Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette, said some of the market's assumptions of improvement in the semiconductor sector were exaggerated. Although most analysts see semiconductor business still weighing on the company, many have included sequential improvement in their financial models, which Buck said may be too strong.
"I still think the $0.45 is suspect," said Buck. "I think that's a best-case scenario."

In addition, analysts said they would watch for the effects of the strong dollar on the company's results, as much of Motorola's business is generated outside the United States. In 1996, international markets accounted for 58 percent of Motorola's total sales.
Shares of Motorola were up 1/4 at 59-3/4 Friday afternoon.
